items.body_md:
Today, the Poolin Technology docket recorded eight motions — Dkts. 155 through 162 — all filed on August 21 and classified in the court's system as "Motion (Generic)." The docket metadata provides no further description of their subject matter, and no secondary reporting has identified their content as of this writing; they cannot be characterized with precision and will require direct review of the filed documents to assess materiality. Eight simultaneous generic motion filings in a single day is unusual in this case and warrants monitoring: depending on their content, they could represent anything from omnibus claim objections to contract rejection motions to creditor-initiated relief requests — all of which would be substantive. Confirmation will require access to the underlying documents on the CM/ECF docket for Case No. 26-18325 (Bankr. D.N.J., Judge O'Hagan).

The August 20 hearing on the Rule 9019 settlement motion (Dkt. 129) — the Elektron Energy settlement scheduled for 11:00 a.m. in Courtroom 2, Trenton, per the order shortening time (Dkt. 137) — has produced no confirming docket entry as of today. The docket reflects a "Hearing Held" entry for August 20, which is consistent with the hearing having proceeded, but no resulting order has appeared. Until an order issues, the Elektron Energy liability — 
a $1,344,788.13 balance owed to Lonestar Dream for the March 2025 to March 2026 period, held in escrow pending release conditions
 — remains unresolved in terms of whether it closes out as a settlement, survives as a cure amount disclosed in Dkt. 149, or persists as a general unsecured claim. That ambiguity has direct bearing on what travels clean to the buyer at closing.


August 21 was the deadline for the assumption and assignment notice, with the assigned contracts schedule and proposed cure amounts
 — executed by Dkt. 149, filed August 19. 
August 27 is the deadline for nonbinding indications of interest
, the next immediate milestone in the sale timeline, followed by 
the September 8 qualified bid deadline, the September 10 auction, and the September 16 sale hearing.
 Counterparties to executory contracts and unexpired leases now hold cure objection rights running from service of Dkt. 149; silence operates as consent to the stated cure amounts, and any undisclosed dispute can encumber title post-closing. The trustee motion (Dkt. 103, hearing October 21) remains pending and unchanged; if granted before the September 16 sale hearing, CRO Michael DuFrayne's authority terminates and an independent trustee assumes control of the auction process. Dkts. 150–154 are BNC certificates of notice — not reported. The immediate priority is identifying the content of Dkts. 155–162 and obtaining the order, if any, that emerged from the August 20 Elektron Energy hearing.

items.lede: On August 20, fifteen subpoenas — Dkts. 118 through 132 — landed on the Omnis Pleasants docket in a single day.
items.body_md:
On August 20, fifteen subpoenas — Dkts. 118 through 132 — landed on the Omnis Pleasants docket in a single day. The docket lines are captioned uniformly as "Subpoena," with no further description of recipients or subject matter visible on their face. Fifteen subpoenas filed simultaneously is not a routine discovery event, even in a contested Chapter 11. The timing and volume place this squarely in the context of the dismissal motion (Dkt. 93) filed by Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum Pleasants: with the objection deadline on that motion set for August 28 and the September 3 final cash collateral and first-day hearings closing in, either the movants or the debtor — most likely the movants given the aggressive posture Lowenstein Sandler has already established through the First Set of Requests for Production (Dkt. 99) — is moving to lock in third-party testimony and document production before the contested hearings. Discovery in support of a dismissal motion or a trustee-appointment request would logically target individuals with knowledge of the circumstances surrounding the Chapter 11 filing itself: the corporate authorization question, the rejected $75.64 million payoff, the governance dispute, and the events preceding the West Virginia state court loss one business day before the petition date.

The practical consequence for the debtor is compounding pressure. The estate is now simultaneously defending against a dismissal/trustee motion with a hard August 28 objection deadline, managing third-party document production in response to Dkt. 99, responding to fifteen subpoenas whose return dates are unknown from the docket face but are presumably keyed to the September 3 hearing complex, and preparing final-hearing submissions on cash collateral and first-day operational orders. Each of those tracks feeds into the others: if subpoena responses surface evidence bearing on corporate authority or the circumstances of the filing, that evidence reaches the dismissal hearing; if the dismissal motion carries, the cash collateral and first-day orders become moot. The debtor's counsel at Young Conaway and Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer will need to manage objections to any subpoenas that are overbroad or seek privileged material while simultaneously briefing the substantive response to Dkt. 93 — a resource allocation problem that is not trivial.

For creditors and claimants, the subpoena barrage is the clearest indicator yet that the August 28 and September 3 proceedings are heading toward full-scale evidentiary contests rather than uncontested hearings. 
The debtor is operating under interim cash-collateral authority while pursuing a sale of substantially all assets, with the final approval of that authority set for September 3; the interim cash-collateral order requires the debtor to continue the sale process and limits any plan absent secured-party consent to one that pays TRAG LLC and RG Energy LLC in full in cash.
 A contested dismissal that succeeds, or a trustee appointment in the alternative, would fundamentally reset those dynamics: a Chapter 11 trustee would step into control of the sale process and could take positions adverse to the debtor's current secured-party relationships. 
If the court declines dismissal, the movants are asking it to appoint an independent Chapter 11 trustee and to vacate the interim cash collateral order.
 Recovery posture for unsecured creditors, including the West Virginia Economic Development Authority — 
the largest creditor at more than $50.8 million, listed as unsecured
 — depends heavily on whether the sale process proceeds on the debtor's terms or is restructured under a trustee. The next concrete milestone is August 27, the objection deadline on the professional retention applications (including Sidley Austin as special regulatory counsel, Dkt. 85), followed by August 28, the objection deadline on the dismissal and trustee motion (Dkt. 93).

items.body_md:
Today, Skillz Platform Inc. filed a Motion to Compel Production of Documents and Certain Deposition Witnesses (Dkt. 73) and a companion Motion to Shorten Notice with respect to that motion (Dkt. 74), both by counsel Michael Neiburg — the most significant escalation on this docket since the deposition notices filed August 11. The motion to compel (Dkt. 73) attaches seven exhibits (Exhibits A through G), signaling a detailed factual record of alleged deficiencies in Papaya's discovery responses: the volume of exhibits is consistent with a party documenting repeated meet-and-confer attempts and specific document categories or witness designations in dispute. The motion to shorten notice (Dkt. 74) is the operative tell: Skillz is not content to wait out a standard notice period and is pressing Judge Walrath to schedule hearing on the underlying motion on an expedited basis, which carries an implicit argument that delay causes prejudice — almost certainly a prejudice tied to an upcoming recognition hearing date. Together, Dkts. 73 and 74 are substantive and important: a motion to compel is an adversarial discovery filing that, in a Chapter 15 context, directly bears on the evidentiary record Skillz needs to contest recognition, and the request for shortened notice signals that Skillz believes a deadline is close enough to make ordinary scheduling inadequate.

The rescheduled hearing notice at Dkt. 71 (filed August 19) is the procedural counterpart worth flagging here — not for its own weight, but because a hearing rescheduling, read alongside Skillz's same-day push to shorten notice on a new motion, suggests that the original hearing calendar has shifted and that Skillz is now racing to complete discovery before a revised hearing date. Dkt. 70, the Order entered August 18 on the heels of Papaya's Certification of Counsel (Dkt. 69), may have set or reset that date; its full text remains unconfirmed in any publicly accessible source and requires PACER review to close that gap. If Dkt. 70 shortened the recognition hearing timeline, that would explain the compressed posture Skillz is projecting today. The deposition notices Skillz filed August 11 (Dkts. 61–62) established that both sides were building records for a contested hearing; Dkts. 73 and 74 confirm that Skillz believes Papaya's production to date is materially incomplete — and that it intends to litigate that deficiency before the recognition hearing rather than absorb the gap.

For creditors and recovery analysis, the significance is structural: Skillz/Firy's ability to contest recognition — and ultimately to resume collection against the approximately $719 million disgorgement judgment plus approximately $10.1 million in fees entered by Judge Cote — depends on the evidentiary record it builds now. 
Judge Walrath's temporary injunction immediately stayed collection and enforcement proceedings against Papaya's U.S. assets, preserving the status quo pending the recognition hearing.
 A motion to compel, if granted, accelerates that evidentiary build and strengthens Skillz's ability to argue at the recognition hearing that the Israeli proceeding does not meet the requirements for recognition — or that the terms of any recognized proceeding should not include continuation of the stay. Papaya's posture — what it has withheld or declined to produce — will become clearer only when the full motion and exhibits are reviewed. The next concrete milestone is Judge Walrath's ruling on the motion to shorten notice (Dkt. 74), which will set the hearing date on the motion to compel (Dkt. 73) and, by extension, define the evidentiary cutoff before the recognition hearing itself. Dkt. 72 (Certificate of Service, August 19) is procedural and routine.

items.body_md:
On August 19, Cowan DeBaets Abrahams & Sheppard LLP filed its own notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit (Dkt. 683), paying the $605 filing fee and entering the appeal alongside Edelson PC and Oppenheim + Zebrak, who had done the same the prior day (Dkt. 682). The two notices are separate filings by separate appellants, not a consolidated submission — meaning the Ninth Circuit will open at least two docketed appeal proceedings arising from the July 20 final approval order, though the court may consolidate them on motion or sua sponte. Both appellant groups were coordinating-counsel or fee-claimant firms rather than class counsel, and together they were the primary drivers of the approximately $75 million supplemental fee request that Anthropic opposed as lacking "scant justification or substantiation" and that Judge Martínez-Olguín resolved as part of the July 20 order setting aside roughly $101.5 million in attorney fees for class counsel. The back-to-back filings, one on each side of the August 19 appeal deadline, confirm the fee outcome rather than the settlement's substantive terms is the operative grievance — though until opening briefs are filed, the precise scope of each appeal remains unconfirmed on the face of the notices.

The structural consequence for class members is unchanged from yesterday but now fully locked: with two sets of appellants on the record, the Effective Date under the settlement agreement cannot arrive, the disbursement portal will not launch, and the roughly 70% first-stage distribution remains in abeyance for the duration of the Ninth Circuit proceedings. 
Payments were to be made in two stages, roughly 70% in the first stage and 30% in the second, as Anthropic will be making settlement payments in installments through September 2027.
 The critical distinction for recovery posture — whether the appeal is confined to fees or extends to final approval itself — will determine whether class members face a full stay of all disbursements or only a hold on funds attributable to disputed counsel compensation. If cabined to fees, there is a plausible argument that undisputed settlement funds could be released to class members during the pendency of the appeal, but that would require either a negotiated arrangement or a court order, neither of which appears on the docket. No stay motion has been filed by any party.

Anthropic's payment obligations run independently of the appeal absent a stay. 
Per the settlement's payment schedule, Anthropic's $450 million first installment (Scheduled Payment 1) falls due September 25, 2026.
 That obligation is not suspended by the filing of a notice of appeal, and no party has moved to stay the judgment. The practical question for the coming weeks is whether any party moves in the district court or the Ninth Circuit for a stay pending appeal, which would require the movant to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits, irreparable harm, balance of equities, and public interest — a high bar for a fee dispute in a settled class action. The next concrete milestone is the Ninth Circuit's assignment of case numbers and issuance of scheduling orders for both appeals, which will establish the opening-brief deadlines and clarify whether the court consolidates the two proceedings.

items.body_md:
On August 19, the Wind Down Trust filed an authorization motion (Dkt. 1321) before Judge Brendan Linehan Shannon in Case No. 24-10070-BLS, Bankr. D. Del. The full text of Dkt. 1321 was not produced in the document pull, so its precise object cannot be confirmed from the primary record. In a post-confirmation liquidating trust at this stage — with claim reconciliation still active across more than 16,000 Crypto Loss Claims, a $4 billion lawsuit against Jump Trading in progress, and the wind-down phase extended through December 31, 2026 — authorization motions typically seek court approval to take a specific estate action outside the ordinary course of the confirmed plan: executing a significant contract, monetizing an asset, entering a litigation settlement, or making a partial distribution. The applicable standard under the confirmed plan and § 363 of the Bankruptcy Code requires a showing that the action is in the best interests of the estate; no secondary reporting on Dkt. 1321 has surfaced to confirm which action is being authorized. Any reader with PACER access should pull the filing directly to confirm the object before acting on it.

Dkt. 1320, the withdrawal notice filed August 18 and covered yesterday, is the only other entry in the window; it carries no additional significance beyond what was already analyzed. Dkts. 1309–1313 and 1319, previously covered, remain as background. The broader distribution posture is unchanged: 
as of the post-confirmation report for the quarter ending March 31, 2026, the Wind Down Trust had distributed nothing to plan creditors, even as the plan administrator continued reconciling more than 16,000 crypto loss claims and pressing a $4 billion lawsuit against Jump Trading as the estate's largest affirmative recovery effort.
 The next concrete milestone on the calendar is December 31, 2026 — the court-extended deadline for the wind-down phase — with any resolution of the Jump Trading litigation or the *Chang v. Terraform Labs Wind Down Trust* adversary proceeding the more material triggers for distribution timing ahead of that date.

items.body_md:
On August 12, at least two parties filed oppositions (Dkts. 51 and 52) and one filed an objection (Dkt. 56) against what the docket labels confirm are distinct contested matters, accompanied by a supporting declaration (Dkt. 53) and a stipulation (Dkt. 57) — the heaviest single day of adversarial activity in this case since the first-day hearing. The docket does not yet identify the targets of those filings by description in the materials available to this desk, but the case context narrows the candidates sharply. The CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43, filed August 5) carried an opposition deadline of August 19 and sought court authorization for insider-adjacent compensation — the CRO, Leslie Gladstone, being named in Dkt. 43's attachments — making it a live target for the U.S. Trustee or judgment creditors. The Manatt employment application (Dkt. 42, filed August 5) is the other obvious target; contested retention applications, particularly where the estate is essentially a litigation-liability vehicle funded by a CEO-owned DIP lender, attract U.S. Trustee scrutiny on disinterestedness and connections. The employment application at Dkt. 49 (filed August 10) is too recent to have drawn a deadline-compliant response by August 12 under standard notice periods. Until the full text of Dkts. 51, 52, 53, 56, and 57 is reviewed on PACER, their precise targets remain unverified; the desk flags this and will confirm at next update. What is clear from the docket structure — two oppositions plus a supporting declaration filed the same day as a separate objection — is that at least two distinct contested matters were briefed simultaneously on August 12, a pattern inconsistent with ordinary course and consistent with coordinated creditor or U.S. Trustee opposition.

The Errors/Deficiencies notice at Dkt. 59 (BNC, August 13) and the Generic Order at Dkt. 60 (August 13) are almost certainly related: the deficiency notice identifies a filing that failed to meet local-rule requirements, and the generic order likely resolves or memorializes the correction. This is procedural and carries no independent weight on recovery, though a deficiency on a retention or compensation filing could slow the authorization clock. Dkts. 54 and 55 are certificates of service, and Dkt. 58 is a proof of service (CSD 3010); all three are filing infrastructure and are omitted. The stipulation at Dkt. 57 is substantive in classification — stipulations in contested Chapter 11 matters affect legal rights — but its substance is unverified; if it reflects an agreed resolution of one of the contested matters briefed the same day, it is material to recovery posture, and the desk will confirm.

The contested posture on these professional-retention and compensation matters matters for creditors beyond the immediate cost. 
The two principal judgments — approximately $245 million in the De la Torre class action and approximately $157 million in the CFPB tribal-lending action — together with roughly $45 million in additional pending litigation and about $5 million in trade debt and professional fees, constitute substantially all of the debtor's prepetition obligations
, against reported assets of $1 million to $10 million. In that context, professional fees and CRO compensation drawn from the estate — funded by a ~$4 million DIP facility 
owned by the debtor's CEO
 — are not administrative minutiae; they directly compress whatever is available to unsecured creditors. Vigorous opposition to these applications signals that at least one party is treating the fee burn as a recovery issue, not a routine creditor courtesy. The next concrete milestone is the August 19 opposition deadline on the CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43), which will either close the briefing on that motion or extend it if further responses arrive — and, depending on the scope of Dkt. 56's objection, the court may consolidate argument on the professional matters at a single hearing.
